questions.stem: A travel insurer uses Claude to triage incoming claims as "straightforward" or "needs investigation". The prompt contains six few-shot examples of straightforward claims, all written in polished, formal English. An analyst notices that claims written informally or by non-native English speakers are flagged for investigation far more often, even when the facts are similar. What is the MOST effective first change?

options.text: Add a line to the system prompt stating that writing style, grammar and fluency must never influence how any claim is triaged or flagged.
Rewrite the six examples to cover varied writing styles and claim types, then re-run evaluation comparing flag rates by style.
Add twenty more examples of well-documented straightforward claims, giving the model a much stronger picture of what a valid claim looks like.
Move triage to the most capable model available, since a stronger model is better at seeing past surface style to the underlying facts.

questions.explanation: Bias can enter through **your own prompt**. When every example of a "good" claim is written in one polished style, the model can learn style as a signal. Anthropic's prompting guidance says examples should be **diverse** and vary enough that Claude doesn't pick up **unintended patterns**. Fix the layer that causes the skew, then **measure by segment** (writing style) to confirm the gap has closed.

whyWrong.A: Instructions to ignore style can reduce skew, but this one leaves the six one-style examples in place (the model still sees polished prose as the pattern of a "good" claim), and nothing measures whether the gap closed.
whyWrong.C: More examples of the same polished style make the unintended pattern stronger, not weaker.
whyWrong.D: A bigger model is the expensive guess. The cause is in the prompt examples, and the fix is still unmeasured.

questions.mindset: Check your own examples for bias before blaming the model, and confirm the fix with a segmented eval.

questions.stem: An agricultural co-operative runs a Claude assistant that answers members' questions using retrieval over its advisory library. Members in several smaller growing regions complain that answers for them are vague or wrong, while members in the main regions are satisfied. Retrieval logs show the library holds very few documents about those smaller regions. Which action BEST addresses the unfair quality gap?

options.text: Instruct the assistant to give every member an equally detailed and specific answer, whichever region they farm in.
Increase the number of chunks retrieved per query, so the assistant has more material to draw on for every question.
Route questions from the smaller regions to a larger, more capable model, so that those members get the strongest reasoning.
Fill the content gap for those regions, add a per-region test set, and have the assistant say when it lacks local guidance.

questions.explanation: The unfairness comes from the **retrieval data layer**: some members are served from a thin corpus. The fix is to close that coverage gap, **measure quality per region** so the gap is visible and tracked, and let the assistant **admit when it has no local information** instead of filling the hole with plausible guesses. Anthropic's hallucination guidance explicitly recommends allowing Claude to say it doesn't know.

whyWrong.A: Demanding detail the knowledge base can't support pushes the model to make up specifics, which makes things worse for those members.
whyWrong.B: More chunks from a corpus that lacks the regional content just adds more irrelevant text to the prompt.
whyWrong.C: A stronger model still has no regional documents to ground its answers. This spends money without fixing the cause.

questions.mindset: Find the layer that underserves a group (here, the corpus), fix it, and measure that group separately.

questions.stem: An insurer is validating a Claude system that recommends approve or refer on home-insurance claims; adjusters make the final call. The plan is to treat five years of past adjuster decisions as ground truth and declare the system fair if it agrees with them at least 95% of the time. An internal audit already found that past approvals were noticeably lower in certain postcodes, with no claim-related reason. What should the architect recommend?

options.text: Replace past decisions with a gold set labelled against the written claims policy by a reviewed, diverse panel, and compare outcomes by postcode.
Keep the historical decisions as ground truth but raise the agreement target to 98%, so the system must match past adjuster decisions even more closely before launch.
Remove postcodes from the model's inputs, then keep measuring agreement with the historical decisions, since the model can no longer see the attribute behind the skew.
Ask Claude to review the five years of historical decisions and correct any it judges unfair, then use the corrected set as the gold standard for evaluation.

questions.explanation: If the labels encode past unfairness, **high agreement with them is evidence of copying the bias**, not of fairness. The eval needs ground truth defined by the **written policy** and checked by people, and results have to be **broken down by segment**, the same counterfactual and segment-based approach Anthropic uses in its own discrimination research.

whyWrong.B: A higher agreement target only rewards matching the biased history more closely.
whyWrong.C: The biased labels are still the target, and other proxies (address, property type) can carry the same signal. Dropping one field doesn't fix the ground truth.
whyWrong.D: Letting the model under test define its own ground truth is circular, and nobody independently checks its corrections.

questions.mindset: Agreement with biased historical decisions is not fairness. Fix the ground truth first.

questions.stem: A property-management company uses Claude to pre-screen rental applications. A leasing officer already makes the final decision on each one, and applicants are told at the start that AI assists the screening. Complaints are rising because declined applicants receive a one-line email with no reason. To fix this quickly, the team proposes a second Claude call made after the officer declines, given only the application and the word "declined", asking the model to "write a reason for this decision". Which approach gives applicants reasons they can trust and contest?

options.text: Keep the post-hoc call, but instruct the model to state only reasons it is highly confident about and to admit when it cannot find a clear reason for the decline.
Have screening score each published criterion with quoted application evidence, require the officer's decline to cite those criteria, and build the letter from that record.
Keep the post-hoc call, and add a second Claude instance that checks each generated reason for plausibility and consistency with the application before sending.
Give any applicant who asks the full screening transcript, including raw model output and the officer's internal notes, so nothing about the decision is hidden.

questions.explanation: A reason written **after** the decision, by a model that was not told why the officer declined, is a **plausible story, not the actual basis**. It can sound convincing and still be wrong, which makes contesting it meaningless. Transparency needs the explanation to come from the **same record the decision was made on**: criterion-level scores grounded in **quoted evidence**, tied to the **published screening criteria**, and referenced by the human who decided. The letter then reports real reasons, and an appeal can check them against the same evidence.

whyWrong.A: Confidence wording does not change the fact that the model is guessing at a decision it did not make. A confidently stated post-hoc reason can still be a fabrication.
whyWrong.C: A second model can only confirm the story is plausible and consistent with the application, not that it was the officer's actual reason. Two models agreeing on a rationalisation is still a rationalisation.
whyWrong.D: Raw transcripts and internal notes are not plain-language reasons tied to criteria, may expose data about third parties or staff, and leave applicants to reverse-engineer the decision themselves.

questions.mindset: An explanation must be the real basis of the decision, recorded when it was made, not a story written afterwards.

questions.stem: A regional news site starts using Claude to draft articles summarising town-council meetings from the official recordings. To save time, drafts go live under a staff reporter's byline after a quick skim. Readers have no way to tell which articles were machine-drafted. The editor-in-chief wants to align with Anthropic's Usage Policy with the least disruption to the workflow. What should the team do?

options.text: Remove bylines from these articles entirely, so that no human reporter is credited with writing content they did not actually produce themselves.
Add a sentence to the site's "About us" page saying that the newsroom uses AI tools in parts of its content production and editing work.
Have an editor review each draft properly before publication, and label the article clearly as produced with AI assistance.
Have Claude fact-check its own draft against the recording before publishing, since a verified draft does not need a separate AI label.

questions.explanation: The Usage Policy treats **journalistic content** as a high-risk use. Two safeguards apply: a **qualified human reviews the content** before publication, and **readers are told AI was involved**. Both fit into the existing editorial workflow with little disruption.

whyWrong.A: Dropping the byline removes the false credit but still doesn't tell readers AI was involved, and there's still no real review.
whyWrong.B: A site-wide note that readers rarely see doesn't disclose AI involvement on the article they're reading.
whyWrong.D: A model checking its own work isn't independent review, and accuracy doesn't replace the duty to disclose.

questions.mindset: For AI-assisted published content: a human reviews it and readers are told AI was involved.

questions.stem: An online community platform uses Claude to flag posts that break its harassment policy; flagged posts are hidden automatically. Members who write in a regional dialect, or in African American English, report that their ordinary posts get hidden much more often than similar posts in standard English. The trust-and-safety lead wants to confirm whether the gap is real and keep members protected while it is fixed. Which TWO actions are MOST appropriate? Choose TWO.

options.text: Build paired test posts with the same meaning written in different language varieties, and compare false-positive rates before changing anything.
Lower the flagging sensitivity for all posts across the platform, so that fewer ordinary posts are hidden whichever variety of English members write in.
Add a system prompt instruction telling the classifier to be tolerant of dialects and informal writing, then ship it, since the model follows instructions well.
Give members a quick appeal to a human moderator for hidden posts, and track how often appeals are overturned for each language variety.
Have the classifier also output a confidence score, and hide posts automatically only when the model reports high confidence in its decision.

questions.explanation: First **measure** the suspected bias with **counterfactual pairs**, where only the language variety changes, and compare **false-positive rates per group** (A). While the fix is in progress, a **human appeal path** limits harm to affected members, and **overturn rates by group** give an ongoing production signal of whether the gap is closing (D).

whyWrong.B: A lower global threshold lets more real harassment through for everyone and may not close the gap between groups.
whyWrong.C: An instruction is an untested guess. Shipping it without measuring tells you nothing about whether the gap closed.
whyWrong.E: A model can be confidently wrong in a consistent way. Self-reported confidence doesn't remove a bias toward one group.

questions.mindset: Confirm bias with counterfactual tests, and give affected people a human appeal while you fix it.

questions.stem: Following data-minimisation advice, a team removed applicants' age and gender from every part of its Claude-assisted loan pre-qualification pipeline. Compliance now asks for evidence that outcomes don't differ unfairly by age or gender, and the team says that, without those fields, it can no longer measure fairness. What is the BEST way to resolve this tension?

options.text: Keep age and gender out of the model's input, but keep them in a separate access-controlled store, on a lawful basis, joined to outcomes only for fairness analysis.
Put age and gender back into the prompt so they can be measured, together with an explicit instruction that the model must never let them influence its recommendation.
Have Claude infer each applicant's likely age and gender from their name and application text, and use those inferred labels to compute the segment metrics compliance needs.
Report overall approval accuracy instead, and explain to compliance that data minimisation makes a segment-level fairness analysis impossible for this pipeline.

questions.explanation: Minimisation and fairness auditing are compatible: **separate what the model sees from what the auditors can measure**. The model never receives the attributes, but outcomes can be joined to them offline, under strict access control and a documented basis, to compute segment metrics. Without that join, a fairness gap could go unseen.

whyWrong.B: This puts the attributes back exactly where they can influence decisions, and depends on an instruction to stop them from doing so.
whyWrong.C: Inferred labels are often wrong and can skew the measurement, and inferring sensitive traits creates new sensitive data and privacy risk.
whyWrong.D: Overall accuracy can hide a gap between groups. Giving up on measurement leaves the risk unexamined.

questions.mindset: Keep protected attributes away from the model but available, under control, for measuring fairness.

questions.stem: An online learning provider uses Claude as an LLM grader to score short written answers against a model answer, and instructors review only scores below the pass mark. A spot check shows the grader gives higher scores to longer answers and to fluent, native-sounding prose, even when two answers contain the same correct points. Learners for whom English is a second language score lower on average. What should the architect do to make grading fair?

options.text: Run the grader three times on each answer and average the scores, so random swings in individual scores are smoothed out and grades become more stable.
Add a second Claude grader that reviews the first grader's score and its stated reasoning, and use the second grader's score whenever the two disagree.
Ask learners to write their answers in simple, standard English and keep them short, so that every answer is graded on a more level playing field.
Give the grader a detailed rubric of content points, have it reason per criterion before scoring, and check it against human-graded answers by language background.

questions.explanation: Anthropic's tips for **LLM-based grading** are to give the grader **detailed, clear rubrics**, to **encourage reasoning** before it scores, and to **test its reliability before scaling** it. Here the grader is itself biased toward length and fluency, so give it a **content rubric** and let it **reason through each criterion before scoring** (chain of thought), which directs it to the points that matter rather than surface style. Then **validate the grader against human-graded answers**, broken down by the group at risk (second-language learners), to confirm the gap has closed.

whyWrong.A: Averaging reduces random variance, but a systematic bias toward length or fluency stays in every run.
whyWrong.B: A second grader built the same way is likely to share the same preference for length and fluency, and nobody checks either grader against human judgment by learner group.
whyWrong.C: This shifts the burden onto learners and says nothing about whether the grader itself is fair.

questions.mindset: An LLM judge is a model too: give it a content rubric and calibrate it against humans, by segment.

questions.stem: A city launches a Claude assistant that helps residents understand whether they might qualify for housing and energy benefits, grounded in the official eligibility rules. Several residents told the assistant they "qualified", skipped steps in the formal application, and were later turned down. The city wants residents to understand what the assistant's answers mean and how far to rely on them. Which TWO changes BEST improve transparency? Choose TWO.

options.text: Add a disclaimer in the page footer saying that the assistant can make mistakes and that residents should always check important information carefully.
Have the assistant refuse every eligibility question and send residents straight to the formal application, to remove any risk of misleading them.
Have answers cite the specific rule sections they rely on and list which facts the assistant could not verify from what the resident said.
Have the assistant give each resident an estimated percentage chance of qualifying, so they can see exactly how confident the answer is.
State in each answer that it is guidance, not an official decision, and show how to reach a caseworker who can make the determination.

questions.explanation: Transparency here means residents can see **what the answer is based on** and **how far it goes**. **Citations to the rule sections** and a list of **unverified facts** show the reasoning and its gaps (C). Making clear that the answer is **guidance, not a determination**, and offering a **path to a caseworker** sets the right level of reliance and gives people a human who can decide (E).

whyWrong.A: A generic footer is easy to miss and doesn't tell residents which parts of a specific answer are uncertain.
whyWrong.B: Refusing everything overcorrects. It removes a useful service instead of making it understandable.
whyWrong.D: A made-up percentage is false precision. It sounds more certain than the model can actually be.

questions.mindset: Make answers show their basis and their limits, and point people to the human who decides.

questions.stem: A health insurer is preparing to launch a Claude-assisted triage step that summarises prior-authorisation requests and suggests a review priority for clinical reviewers. The ML lead proposes citing the general bias-benchmark results published for the model as the launch's fairness evidence, so that launch isn't delayed. Governance wants evidence that will stand up to regulators and patient advocates. What should the architect recommend?

options.text: Accept the published benchmark results as sufficient evidence, because they were produced by the model provider and cover a wide range of demographic groups.
Let the engineering team choose a single fairness metric now and launch, then refine the metric later once real traffic shows where problems actually occur.
Agree relevant patient segments and acceptable gap thresholds with compliance, clinical experts and patient advocates, then test on this task's data.
Delay the launch until a model version is available whose published benchmarks show no measurable bias across any of the demographic groups tested.

questions.explanation: General benchmarks measure the model in **generic settings**, not **this task, data and workflow**. Fairness evidence that holds up needs **task-specific success criteria**: which segments matter and what gap is acceptable, agreed with the **stakeholders accountable for and affected by the outcome**, then measured on representative task data. Anthropic's guidance on defining success criteria and building evals emphasises being task-specific.

whyWrong.A: A general benchmark doesn't show how your prompts, data and priority rules treat your patients.
whyWrong.B: An engineering-only metric picked under time pressure leaves out the people who are accountable and affected, and the risk falls on patients while it gets refined.
whyWrong.D: No model shows zero bias on every test. Waiting for perfection blocks the work without producing task-specific evidence.

questions.mindset: Fairness is defined with stakeholders and proven on your own task, not borrowed from a generic benchmark.
